answers.answer: The client asks the stub resolver. The stub sends that query to one recursive resolver and does not itself follow delegations to the authoritative name server. The deck does not say the stub asks the recursive resolver to follow delegations, and it does not describe the queries or delegation steps by which the recursive resolver contacts the authoritative name server. It says only that a recursive resolver returns an answer or an error, and that on this first lookup nothing relevant is cached, so the recursive resolver obtains the answer from the authoritative name server. The authoritative name server answers from its zone data, the records it stores for that part of the namespace. That same recursive resolver then stores a copy. When a second client asks the same recursive resolver before the copy expires, that resolver answers the second lookup from its cached copy and does not contact the authoritative name server again. That answer is stored data, a copy the resolver kept, not a live read of the zone. The DNS step is the lookup, which returns resource records and only supplies addressing data. The HTTP step is separate: the client then connects to an address from those records and sends GET /notes. The DNS response does not proxy GET /notes, does not check whether the Notes API is healthy on this request, and does not store the HTTP response. After the name has resolved, the connection can still be refused.

A recursive resolver returns an answer or an error. The authoritative name server answers from its zone data, the records it stores for that part of the namespace. On this first lookup nothing relevant is cached, so the recursive resolver obtains the answer from the authoritative name server.

That resolver stores a copy. When a second client asks the same recursive resolver before the copy expires, the resolver answers from its cached copy and does not contact the authoritative name server again. A cached answer is stored data, not a live read of the zone.
The DNS lookup and the HTTP request are different steps. The lookup returns resource records. The client then connects to an address from those records and sends GET /notes.
The DNS response does not proxy GET /notes, does not check whether the Notes API is healthy on this request, and does not store the HTTP response.
A successful lookup only supplies addressing data. The connection can still be refused, the response can still be lost, or the API can still return an HTTP error.

answers.answer: In this example api.notes.example is a CNAME, an alias, of origin.notes.example. The CNAME contains that canonical name. It does not contain an IP address, so the lookup cannot stop at the alias, and the resolver continues the DNS lookup at origin.notes.example. An A record carries one IPv4 address, such as 192.0.2.10. An AAAA record carries one IPv6 address, such as 2001:db8::10. Yes: the resolver follows the alias and can return the CNAME together with the address record it found. The client connects only after an address record has been obtained. The two A records, 192.0.2.10 and 192.0.2.20, are a set of addresses for one name, not an ordered health-aware assignment of HTTP requests. The order of records in that set is not significant, and it need not be preserved. That order is not health-aware distribution of HTTP requests. This ordinary DNS answer does not check which address accepts the Notes API. If the client connects to 192.0.2.20 and that address accepts no connections, DNS was not required to omit it; the client can attempt that address and the connection can fail.

answers.answer: At 12:20 the first resolver, resolver A, may still return 192.0.2.10 because its TTL has not expired. The remaining TTL allows that cache to keep reusing its own copy until the countdown reaches zero at 13:00. A TTL is the time one cache may reuse its copy before the source should be consulted again, and it is a maximum for that copy: a cache may discard the copy sooner. This TTL does not promise that the authoritative change at 12:10 updates every resolver, and it does not promise that every resolver drops 192.0.2.10 at the same instant. An authoritative change does not rewrite other caches, and resolvers that stored the old address at different times do not drop it at the same instant. At 13:02, resolver A's countdown has reached zero, so it should consult the source again, while resolver B may still reuse 192.0.2.10 until 13:05 because its copy was stored at 12:05. If a resolver's TTL has reached zero and it cannot get an authoritative refresh, reuse of the expired address is allowed. That reuse is not required of every resolver, and it is not forbidden.

evidence.quote: A TTL is the time one cache may reuse its copy of an answer before the source should be consulted again. It is a maximum for that copy: a cache may discard the copy sooner. An authoritative change does not rewrite other caches. Resolvers that stored the old address at different times do not drop it at the same instant.
At 12:10 the authoritative record becomes 192.0.2.30, and nobody flushes the resolvers. At 12:20 resolver A may still return 192.0.2.10 because its TTL has not expired.
At 13:02, resolver A's countdown has reached zero, so it should consult the source again. Resolver B may still reuse 192.0.2.10 until 13:05.
If a resolver cannot get an authoritative refresh when the TTL expires, it is allowed to reuse the expired address. That reuse is not required of every resolver.
A TTL limits one cached copy. It does not update every resolver at once.

answers.answer: A timeout means no DNS answer arrived. It does not prove that api.notes.example does not exist. SERVFAIL means a server reported that it could not process the query. Neither the timeout nor SERVFAIL proves that the name does not exist, and neither proves that the Notes API process is down. Client A can fail to reach the healthy API because the client still has no address, so it cannot open the connection; a failed lookup can make the healthy API unreachable from that client. NXDOMAIN means the queried name does not exist. A resolver can cache that name error and keep returning it after the name is added, until the negative answer expires, so Client B, looking up again through the same resolver before that expiry, can still be given the cached name error and treat the name as absent. The time limit that allows that negative answer to be reused is the negative-caching TTL carried with that name-error answer: the lesser of the zone SOA record's TTL and its MINIMUM field. It is not the TTL of an address record, because no address record was returned. A different name that exists but has no record of the requested address type, including no A or AAAA record, is a no-data answer, not NXDOMAIN. That negative answer can also be cached.

NXDOMAIN means the queried name does not exist. A resolver can cache that name error and keep returning it after the name is added, until the negative answer expires.

The reuse limit is the negative-caching TTL carried with that name-error answer: the lesser of the zone SOA record's TTL and its MINIMUM field. It is not the TTL of an address record, because no address record was returned.

answers.answer: For a planned cutover, lower the TTL first while the published address is still 192.0.2.10. Then wait at least 86400 seconds, so caches that stored the old answer under that lifetime can expire and observe the shorter TTL. Only then change the authoritative address to 192.0.2.30. The wait follows the previously cached TTL because resolvers have already cached 192.0.2.10 with a TTL of 86400 seconds, and lowering the TTL does not rewrite countdowns already stored; those caches can keep returning 192.0.2.10 until the TTL they stored ends. Changing the address without waiting out the old TTL, or publishing the short TTL only at the moment of the address change, leaves holders of the old cached TTL on 192.0.2.10 until that cached lifetime ends. Editing the authoritative record does not rewrite answers already stored in caches. After the wait and the address change, the team cannot claim that every Notes client has stopped using 192.0.2.10, because some caches can still retain or reuse a stale answer. A client that wants 192.0.2.30 still depends on a DNS lookup to learn it, so DNS remains an extra dependency in front of the new address.

After the wait and the change, do not claim that every Notes client has stopped using 192.0.2.10. Some caches can still retain or reuse a stale answer. A client that wants 192.0.2.30 still depends on a DNS lookup to learn it, so DNS remains an extra dependency in front of the new address.

answers.answer: Yes. Installed Notes clients should keep a stable hostname, api.notes.example, rather than deleting that name and shipping 192.0.2.10 and 192.0.2.20 inside the app. When the address must change, that same name can return a new address without shipping a new IP address to every installed client. Each cache may still serve the old address until its TTL allows a refresh. Hard-coding today's addresses does not provide that later change. Those two address records still fail to replace a component that distributes each HTTP request and avoids unhealthy backends because two address records are only a set of addresses: they do not health-check backends, and they do not distribute each HTTP request. One job that remains outside DNS is choosing a healthy backend for an HTTP request. Proxying that request is also outside DNS. Keep the name so clients can follow a planned address change, and add a separate component when the design needs per-request selection of a healthy backend.

evidence.quote: Installed Notes clients should keep a stable hostname, api.notes.example. When the address must change, that same name can return a new address without shipping a new IP address to every installed client. Each cache may still serve the old address until its TTL allows a refresh. Hard-coding today's addresses does not provide that later change.

Two address records, such as 192.0.2.10 and 192.0.2.20, are only a set of addresses. They do not health-check backends, and they do not distribute each HTTP request. Choosing a healthy backend for an HTTP request, or proxying that request, remains outside DNS.
Keep the name so clients can follow a planned address change. Add a separate component when the design needs per-request selection of a healthy backend.
A stable name absorbs an address change. It does not check health or balance requests.
